text: A plesiosaur was a sea [[reptile|reptile]] that lived from about 203 to 66 million years ago, alongside the dinosaurs. Most had a small head, a long neck, a broad, flat body, four big flippers and a short tail. Some were the size of a person. The biggest were longer than a school bus.

They breathed air, so they had to come to the surface. They ate fish, squid-like animals and shellfish. They lived in oceans all over the world and died out at the same time as the big dinosaurs, after a giant [[asteroid|asteroid]] hit Earth 66 million years ago.

sec.t:
Lyme Regis is a small town on England's south coast, where the cliffs are packed with [[fossil|fossils]]. [[@mary-anning|Mary Anning]] grew up there, poor, selling fossils to tourists to help her family. In 1823, when she was 24, she found an almost complete plesiosaur skeleton.

It looked so odd that the French expert Georges Cuvier wondered if someone had joined two animals together. No living creature had a neck that long. Scientists studied it at a meeting in London and agreed it was real. Cuvier accepted it. But as a woman, Anning was not allowed to join the Geological Society, and for many years others took credit for her finds. Her plesiosaur is now kept at the Natural History Museum in London.

The plesiosaur group had two main body shapes. Elasmosaurs had extremely long necks. *Elasmosaurus*, found in Kansas, had a neck about 7 metres long with more than 70 bones in it. Elasmosaurs had more neck bones than any other animals we know of. A giraffe has just seven.

Pliosaurs had the opposite shape: short necks and enormous heads, with teeth like bananas. Some had skulls more than 2 metres long. They were among the top hunters of the ancient seas, eating fish, other reptiles and even smaller plesiosaurs.

sec.h: A head on the wrong end

sec.t:
For a long time, scientists wondered how plesiosaurs had young. Their flippers would have made it almost impossible to crawl onto a beach and lay eggs like a [[@sea-turtles|sea turtle]]. In 2011, researchers described a fossil plesiosaur from Kansas with a single large baby inside it. This showed that plesiosaurs gave birth to live young in the water, much as whales and dolphins do today.

The baby was big compared with its mother, which suggests plesiosaurs had one large baby at a time and may have looked after it.

Some people believe the Loch Ness Monster in Scotland is a surviving plesiosaur. The most famous photo of "Nessie", from 1934, was revealed in 1994 to be a model on a toy submarine. Loch Ness also only formed after the last ice age, about 10,000 years ago, and its cold, fresh water could not feed a family of large reptiles. Plesiosaurs left no fossils younger than 66 million years. As far as scientists can tell, the last one swam a very long time ago.

sec.h: गर्मी में आराम करने वाले जंगल
sec.t:
भारत के ज़्यादातर जंगल उष्णकटिबंधीय पर्णपाती हैं। "पर्णपाती" का मतलब है कि पेड़ साल के कुछ हिस्से में पत्ते गिरा देते हैं। मध्य भारत में मानसून से पहले के गर्म, सूखे महीने पूरी की पूरी पहाड़ियों को भूरा और नंगा कर देते हैं।

ये जंगल सागौन और साल जैसे क़ीमती पेड़ों का घर हैं, और भारत के ज़्यादातर वन्यजीवों का भी, जिनमें बहुत-से बाघ शामिल हैं। मध्य प्रदेश के कान्हा, पेंच और बांधवगढ़ पर्णपाती जंगल हैं। ये [[@bamboo|बाँस]] से भी भरे हैं, जो असल में एक विशाल घास है।

राजस्थान और गुजरात में बारिश कम होती है, और सिर्फ़ मज़बूत पेड़ बचते हैं। बबूल, खेजड़ी और बेर के काँटेदार जंगलों की पत्तियाँ छोटी और जड़ें गहरी होती हैं, जो ज़मीन के बहुत नीचे के पानी तक पहुँचती हैं।

हिमालय में चढ़ो तो ऊँचाई के साथ जंगल बदलते जाते हैं। निचली ढलानों पर चीड़ और बाँज उगते हैं। ऊपर देवदार, फ़र और स्प्रूस आते हैं, फिर बुरांश, जो वसंत में लाल खिलता है। लगभग 3,500 मीटर से ऊपर पेड़ों की जगह ऊँचाई वाले घास के मैदान (बुग्याल) ले लेते हैं।

कीचड़ वाले तटों पर [[@mangroves|मैंग्रोव]] खारे ज्वारीय पानी में जड़ें डाले उगते हैं। भारत और बांग्लादेश में फैला सुंदरबन धरती के सबसे बड़े मैंग्रोव जंगलों में से एक है, और उन बाघों का घर है जो एक टापू से दूसरे टापू तक तैरते हैं।

sec.h: बढ़ रहे हैं या घट रहे हैं?
sec.t:
हर दो साल में भारतीय वन सर्वेक्षण उपग्रह तस्वीरों से देश के पेड़ों का फैलाव नापता है। हाल की रिपोर्टें दिखाती हैं कि भारत में वन और पेड़ धीरे-धीरे बढ़ रहे हैं। सुनने में यह अच्छी ख़बर है, और बहुत-सी जगहों पर है भी।

पर कुछ वैज्ञानिक और संरक्षण संगठन सावधान रहने को कहते हैं। उपग्रह पेड़ों से घना हर टुकड़ा गिन लेते हैं, इसलिए चाय बाग़ान, फलों के बग़ीचे और एक ही पेड़ के तेज़ी से बढ़ने वाले बाग़ान भी जंगल गिने जा सकते हैं। यूकेलिप्टस का बाग़ान पक्षियों, कीड़ों और सैकड़ों पौधों की प्रजातियों से भरे किसी पुराने क़ुदरती जंगल से बहुत अलग है। इस बीच कुछ पुराने जंगल अब भी खदानों, बाँधों और सड़कों के लिए काटे जा रहे हैं। इसलिए जानकार दो सवाल पूछते हैं: जंगल कितना है, और किस तरह का है? इसी से तय होती है असली [[biodiversity|जैव विविधता]]।

लाखों लोग जंगलों में या उनके पास रहते हैं और जलावन, फल, शहद, दवाओं और चराई के लिए उन पर निर्भर हैं। बहुत-से आदिवासी समुदाय पीढ़ियों से जंगलों की देखभाल करते आए हैं, और कुछ गाँव ऐसे पवित्र उपवन (देवबन) बचाकर रखते हैं जहाँ एक भी पेड़ नहीं काटा जा सकता।

1970 के दशक में हिमालय में गाँव की औरतें लकड़ी काटने वालों को रोकने के लिए पेड़ों से लिपट गईं, और यह [[@chipko|चिपको]] आंदोलन बना। आज वन अधिकारी भारत के जंगलों को कई क़िस्मों में बाँटते हैं, उस पद्धति के हिसाब से जो हैरी चैंपियन और एस. के. सेठ ने 1968 में छापी थी। इसके 16 मुख्य समूह, गीले सदाबहार से लेकर ऊँचाई वाली झाड़ियों तक, आज भी यह योजना बनाने में इस्तेमाल होते हैं कि जंगलों को कैसे बचाया जाए।

text: A lake becomes salty when water flows in but can't flow out. Rivers and streams always carry small amounts of [[dissolve|dissolved]] salts, picked up from rocks and soil. In most lakes, that water keeps moving, out through a river to the sea, so the salts are carried away.

Some lakes have no outlet. The only way water leaves is by evaporating into the air, and when water evaporates, the salt stays behind. Over thousands of years, the salt builds up and the lake becomes salty. Hot, dry places, where [[evaporation|evaporation]] is strong, have the saltiest lakes.

sec.t:
All river water has a little salt in it, though too little to taste. Rain falling on rock slowly dissolves tiny amounts of minerals, and rivers carry them along. The same process, over billions of years, made the [[@why-sea-salty|sea salty]].

A lake with no outlet is like a smaller version of the ocean. It collects the salts from every stream that feeds it. The [[@water-cycle|water cycle]] lifts pure water out of it as vapour and leaves the salts behind, year after year.

The [[@dead-sea|Dead Sea]] lies between Jordan, Israel and the West Bank. Its shore is [[@extreme-lowest-point|about 430 m below sea level]], the lowest land on Earth. The Jordan River flows in, but nothing flows out, and the desert sun is fierce.

Its water is about ten times saltier than the ocean. That makes it so dense that people float with their heads, arms and feet sticking out. Salt crystals form white crusts along the shore. The lake is shrinking, though, by about a metre a year, as people take water from the Jordan River for farms and towns.

Sambhar Lake, near [[@jaipur|Jaipur]] in Rajasthan, is India's largest inland salt lake. In [[@monsoon|the monsoon]], it fills with water from streams. In the dry months, it shrinks and leaves behind a shining white crust.

Salt has been collected from Sambhar for centuries, and the lake still produces salt today. The lake is a protected [[wetland|wetland]], and in winter it is visited by thousands of [[@flamingos-pink|flamingos]], which feed on tiny shrimp and [[algae|algae]].

[[@india-wonder-lonar|Lonar Lake]] in Maharashtra fills a round [[crater|crater]] made when a [[@meteorites|meteorite]] slammed into the ancient [[lava|lava]] rock of the Deccan, many thousands of years ago. The lake has no outlet, and its water is both salty and strongly alkaline, a bit like water mixed with baking soda.

In June 2020, the lake turned bright pink. Scientists studied the water and suggested that a bloom of salt-loving microbes had multiplied as the water level dropped and the water became saltier. After the monsoon rains came, the colour faded.

[[@india-wonder-pangong|Pangong Tso]], high in [[@ladakh|Ladakh]] on the border between India and China, sits more than 4,000 m above sea level. Its eastern end is fresh, but the western part, in India, is slightly salty, because the lake has no outlet.

In winter, even this salty water freezes over. In summer, its colour changes through the day, from blue to green to grey, as the light shifts.

text: Nobody knows exactly. [[astronomer|Astronomers]] can't count every galaxy, so they count the ones in small patches of sky and multiply. Their best estimates for the part of the universe we can see run from a few hundred billion galaxies up to about [[@large-numbers-names|two trillion]].

Each galaxy is a vast family of stars, gas and dust held together by [[gravity|gravity]]. Our own, the [[@milky-way|Milky Way]], has hundreds of billions of stars. Multiply that by hundreds of billions of galaxies, and the number of stars becomes so big that it's hard to write down.

sec.t:
A hundred years ago, many astronomers thought the Milky Way was the whole universe. Faint, fuzzy patches in the sky, called [[@nebulae|nebulae]], were thought to be clouds of gas inside it. Others argued that some were separate "island universes", very far away. In 1920, two American astronomers held a famous public debate about it in Washington.

The answer came from Mount Wilson Observatory in California. In 1923 and 1924, Edwin Hubble found a special kind of flickering star in the Andromeda [[nebula|nebula]]. These stars pulse at a speed that reveals how bright they really are. Comparing that with how faint it looked told him its distance. It was far outside the Milky Way. Andromeda was a whole galaxy.

That method came from Henrietta Swan Leavitt, who worked at the Harvard College Observatory measuring stars on glass photographic plates. She was paid very little and given little credit in her lifetime. Her discovery became one of the most useful tools in astronomy.

In December 1995, astronomers aimed the [[@hubble|Hubble Space Telescope]] at a tiny patch of sky near the Big Dipper that seemed empty. They took exposures for about ten days. The picture, called the Hubble Deep Field, showed around 3,000 galaxies. Later deep pictures by Hubble and the James Webb Space Telescope found even more.

Then came the maths. If one tiny patch holds thousands of galaxies, and the whole sky is millions of times bigger, the total must be in the hundreds of billions. This is [[@estimation|estimation]], the same trick you would use to guess the number of people at a cricket match from one section of the stands.

In 2016, a team led by Christopher Conselice estimated about two trillion galaxies, counting many small, faint ones too dim to see. Later measurements of how dark space really is, using NASA's New Horizons spacecraft far out beyond Pluto, suggested the true number may be lower. The argument continues.

India's space telescope [[@space-telescopes-india|AstroSat]], launched by [[@isro-missions|ISRO]] in 2015, can see [[ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] light, which our [[atmosphere|atmosphere]] blocks. In 2020, Indian astronomers reported that it had picked up ultraviolet light from a galaxy about 9.3 billion [[@light-years|light-years]] away. That light left its galaxy long before Earth even existed.

text: Seeds fly by being shaped to catch the wind. A plant can't move, so if its seeds just fell straight down, the young plants would have to grow in their parent's shade, competing with it for light, water and soil. Seeds that travel get a better start.

Many plants solve this by building seeds that fall slowly. Some have fluffy [[@parachutes|parachutes]], like the dandelion. Some have a wing that makes them spin like a [[@helicopters|helicopter]], like the maple. A few have wide, papery wings that glide like aeroplanes. The slower a seed falls, the farther a breeze can carry it.

st.prompt: A maple seed has one wing, like half of a propeller. What does it do when it falls?

options.t: Drops straight down like a stone
Spins round and round, falling slowly
Floats upwards on its own

st.reveal: The wing makes the seed spin as it falls, like a helicopter blade. A small whirl of air forms along the front edge of the spinning wing, which gives extra lift and slows the fall, so the wind has more time to carry it away.

sec.t:
Blow on a dandelion clock and a hundred tiny parachutes drift away. Each seed hangs below a crown of about 100 fine bristles.

For years, scientists weren't sure how such a gappy parachute worked. In 2018, researchers in Scotland filmed dandelion seeds in a wind tunnel. They found that air flowing through the bristles forms a stable ring of swirling air, a [[vortex|vortex]], just above the crown. That ring lowers the pressure above the seed and helps hold it up. A dandelion seed can stay aloft long enough to travel a kilometre or more on a breezy day.

India has its own fluffy fliers. The aak, or madar, a tough roadside shrub, splits open to release flat brown seeds with tufts of silky white hair. In spring, the silk-cotton tree, or semal, drops pods that burst into clouds of fluff. People have used semal fluff to stuff pillows.

sec.h: The seed that inspired a plane
sec.t:
In the [[@rainforests|rainforests]] of Southeast Asia, a climbing plant called the Javan cucumber, *Alsomitra macrocarpa*, grows high in the trees. Its seeds have thin, curved wings about 13 cm wide. Released, they glide smoothly in wide circles, sometimes a long way from the parent.

In the early 1900s, the Austrian aircraft designer Igo Etrich studied these seeds and used their shape for his early [[@gliders|gliders]] and planes. Seeds were teaching flight before most people had seen an aeroplane. Their gentle glide is a lot like a well-made [[@paper-planes|paper plane]].

Seeds that travel can reach empty ground after a fire, a flood or a landslide, and start new plants there. Some find new islands. After the volcano of Krakatoa in Indonesia erupted in 1883 and wiped out life on the remaining island, ferns and grasses with wind-blown spores and seeds were among the first to return.

Not all seeds fly. [[@coconut|Coconuts]] float across seas. Many fruits are eaten by birds, which drop the seeds far away, which is how many [[@banyan|banyan]] trees get planted. Burrs hitch rides on animal fur. The garden balsam fires its seeds out of pods that burst when touched. Flying is just one of the ways plants have found to [[@plants-move|move]] without walking.

text: The white lines are contrails, short for [[condensation|condensation]] trails. When a plane's [[@plane-jet|jet engine]] burns kerosene fuel, it gives off hot gases full of water vapour. High in the sky, about 8 to 12 km up, the air is usually colder than minus 40°C. The vapour cools in an instant, condenses around tiny soot particles and freezes into ice crystals.
The result is a long, thin cloud stretching behind the plane. It is the same thing that happens when your warm breath turns into a white puff on a cold morning, only bigger, colder and a lot higher.

st.prompt: What are contrails made of?

options.t: Tiny ice crystals formed from water vapour in the engine exhaust
Smoke from burning fuel
Chemicals sprayed on purpose from the plane

st.reveal: Jet exhaust is hot and full of water vapour. In the freezing air high up, the vapour quickly condenses and freezes into ice crystals, forming a narrow cloud, the same way your breath turns white on a cold morning.

sec.t:
It seems odd that burning fuel makes water. But jet fuel is made of hydrogen and carbon. When it burns, the hydrogen joins with oxygen from the air to form water. Burning 1 kg of fuel makes more than 1 kg of water vapour.

A big airliner can burn several tonnes of fuel an hour, so it releases tonnes of water vapour every hour into the high, freezing air. Look closely at a fresh contrail and you may see a short clear gap right behind the engines. The exhaust needs a moment to cool before the ice appears.

sec.h: Why some vanish and some stay

sec.t:
This is where scientists are still working things out. During the day, contrails reflect some sunlight back into space, which cools the ground a little. At night, they act like a blanket, trapping heat that would otherwise escape. Overall, most studies find that contrails warm the Earth.

A large 2021 study suggested the warming from contrail clouds may be larger than the warming from the [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]] that planes release, at least in the short term. Other researchers say the uncertainty is still big. What is clear is that they matter for [[@climate-change|climate change]].

A surprising finding is that a small share of flights makes most of the warming contrails, those passing through cold, moist patches of air. If pilots fly a little higher or lower, they can avoid these patches.

In 2023, Google and American Airlines tested using computer predictions to steer some flights away from contrail-forming air. They reported about half as many contrails, with only a small increase in fuel. More trials are under way.

Some people online claim that lasting trails are "chemtrails", chemicals sprayed in secret. Scientists who looked at the evidence found nothing to support this. It is a good example of why [[@fake-news|fake news]] spreads: the trails are real and visible, but the explanation is wrong.

During the Second World War, contrails were a danger for pilots, because the white lines gave away the position of bomber formations to the enemy. Planes still make them today, and on a busy day over India's air routes, you can sometimes see several criss-crossing the blue at once. They form at the same heights where powerful [[@jet-streams|jet streams]] can blow at hundreds of kilometres an hour, which is why a trail can bend or drift within minutes.

text: The Bloop was a very loud, very low underwater sound recorded in 1997 by NOAA, the American agency that studies the oceans and the air. It lasted about a minute and rose in pitch, a bit like a giant "bloooop". Several underwater microphones picked it up, some more than 5,000 km from its source.

Because it was so loud and so mysterious, many people guessed it came from an unknown sea creature. NOAA scientists later concluded it was almost certainly an icequake: the sound of a huge iceberg cracking or breaking off Antarctica.

st.prompt: What do NOAA scientists now think made the Bloop?

options.t: Huge pieces of ice cracking near Antarctica
A giant unknown sea creature
A secret submarine

st.reveal: Scientists recorded many icequakes off Antarctica over the following years. Their sounds look very much like the Bloop on a spectrogram, a picture of sound. An animal would have to be far bigger than a blue whale to make that much noise.

n.certNote: NOAA scientists say the Bloop matches the sound of icequakes, when huge icebergs crack or break off Antarctica. Because nobody saw the event, this is the best explanation rather than a proven one.

d.try: Fill a sink or bucket with water. Put one ear against the side of the bucket while a friend taps two spoons together under the water, then taps them in the air. Which sounds louder and clearer? Sound travels about four times faster in water than in air.
myth: The Bloop proved there is a gigantic unknown animal in the deep sea.

The sound was far too powerful for any known animal, even a blue whale. The best explanation is ice cracking near Antarctica, which makes similar sounds that scientists have recorded many times since.

sec.t:
During the Cold War, the US Navy placed underwater microphones, called [[hydrophone|hydrophones]], across the oceans to track enemy submarines. Later, scientists at NOAA used some of these and their own hydrophones to listen for natural sounds, like undersea volcanoes, earthquakes and whales.

The ocean is surprisingly noisy. [[@whale-songs|Whales sing]], shrimps snap, ships rumble and the sea floor creaks. Scientists turn these sounds into pictures called spectrograms, which show pitch and loudness over time.

How can a sound travel so far? The ocean has a hidden layer, often about 1,000 metres down, called the SOFAR channel. In this layer, the temperature and pressure work together to bend sound waves back towards the middle, so they don't escape up or down.

Sound can bounce along this layer for thousands of kilometres, losing very little energy. Some whales may use it to call to each other across ocean basins. It was this layer that carried the Bloop so far.

The US Navy discovered the channel during the Second World War. In tests, a small explosive set off in the channel could be heard thousands of kilometres away. Sailors even planned to use it to find airmen lost at sea, who would drop a small charge that sank to the right depth and went bang.

Over the next years, NOAA put hydrophones closer to Antarctica. They recorded many sounds made by ice. When huge icebergs crack, scrape the sea floor or break away from ice shelves, they create long, rising sounds called icequakes.

On spectrograms, many of these looked just like the Bloop. By the mid-2000s, NOAA scientists had concluded that the Bloop was most likely an icequake from Antarctic ice. [[@glaciers|Glaciers]] and ice shelves breaking up can release huge amounts of energy, easily enough to be heard across an ocean.

The Bloop's location became famous for another reason. It was fairly close to a spot in the Pacific where the American writer H. P. Lovecraft had placed the sunken city of his made-up sea monster, Cthulhu, in a 1928 story. Fans loved the coincidence.

But an animal loud enough to make the Bloop would have to be far bigger than a blue whale, the largest animal ever known. Real deep-sea giants, like the [[@giant-squid|giant squid]], don't make loud calls at all.

The Bloop isn't the only odd noise. Others have nicknames like "Upsweep", "Julia" and "Slow Down". Upsweep, heard since 1991, may come from volcanic activity. Julia and Slow Down seem to come from ice too.

Sounds from space have puzzled scientists in the same way. In 1977, a radio telescope in the USA picked up a strong signal nobody could explain, a mystery still debated as the [[@mystery-wow-signal|Wow! signal]].

text: Camels survive the desert by being extremely careful with water. Their [[@kidneys|kidneys]] make very little urine, and their dung comes out so dry that people use it as fuel. Their noses catch moisture from each breath before it escapes.

They also let their bodies heat up. During the day, a camel's temperature can climb by about 6°C before it starts sweating, saving water. At night, it cools down again. A camel can lose about a quarter of its body weight in water and still be fine. A person who lost that much would be in great danger.
When it does find water, a thirsty camel can gulp about 100 litres in around a quarter of an hour.

st.prompt: What is stored inside a camel's hump?

options.t: Water
Fat
Extra bone

st.reveal: The hump is a lump of fat that the camel can live off when food is scarce. Keeping fat in one place, instead of spread under the skin, also lets heat escape more easily from the rest of its body. A hungry camel's hump goes floppy and can lean to one side.

sec.t:
Camels have two rows of long eyelashes and a thin third eyelid that wipes sand from their eyes like a windscreen wiper. Their ears are lined with hair, and their nostrils can close tight during a sandstorm.

Their feet are wide, with two toes joined by a tough, leathery pad that spreads out on soft sand. Thick pads on their knees and chest let them kneel on burning ground. Their lips are tough enough to munch thorny desert plants that other animals avoid.

Even their [[@blood|blood]] is special. Camel red blood cells are oval, not round. They keep flowing when the blood thickens from [[@thirst|thirst]], and they can swell when the camel drinks a lot without bursting.

Camels have carried people and goods across the [[@desert-life|Thar Desert]] for centuries. The Raika herders of Rajasthan have bred and cared for camels for generations. Every year, thousands of camels are traded at [[@india-wonder-pushkar|the Pushkar fair]], and Rajasthan made the camel its state animal in 2014.

India's Border Security Force still patrols parts of the desert on camels, and its camel band marches in [[@republic-day-parade|the Republic Day parade]]. In Kutch, Gujarat, Kharai camels do something even stranger: they swim out to islands of mangroves to graze.

But camel numbers in India are falling fast as roads and tractors replace them. The 2019 count found about 2.5 lakh, around a third fewer than in 2012. In Bikaner, a government research centre is working on camel milk, cheese and even [[@ice-cream-freezing|ice cream]], so that keeping camels pays.

{{story:silk-road}}

Two-humped Bactrian camels live in the cold deserts of Central Asia, where winters are freezing and summers are scorching. For centuries they carried silk, spices and tea along the [[@silk-road|Silk Road]].

A few still live in the Nubra Valley of [[@ladakh|Ladakh]], [[descendant|descendants]] of camels from the old [[caravan|caravans]] that crossed the mountains. Tourists now ride them over sand dunes surrounded by snowy peaks. In winter, they grow thick, shaggy coats that they shed in great clumps in spring.

Here is a surprise. The camel family began in North America, around 40 million years ago. Some early camels were no bigger than a goat. Over millions of years, some crossed a land bridge into Asia, and others moved into South America, where their relatives the llamas and alpacas still live. The camels left in North America died out thousands of years ago.

Camels came back for a short time. In the 1850s, the US Army brought dozens of camels to [[@texas|Texas]] to carry supplies across the dry Southwest. The plan was dropped after the American Civil War. In Australia, camels brought by cameleers from British India and Afghanistan in the 1800s were later set loose. Today hundreds of thousands roam wild across its outback.

text: A moving car has a lot of energy because it's heavy and fast. To stop it, that energy has to go somewhere. Brakes turn it into heat, using [[@friction|friction]].

When you press the brake pedal, you push a [[piston|piston]] that squeezes a special oil called brake fluid in a set of pipes. The fluid carries the push to all four wheels. At each wheel, the push presses hard, rough pads against a metal disc or drum that spins with the wheel. The rubbing slows the wheel down and heats the brakes.
The car slows, the brakes warm up, and the energy that was speed has become heat that drifts away into the air.

st.prompt: A car going 50 km/h brakes to a stop. Where does all its movement energy go?

options.t: It disappears
It turns into heat in the brakes
It goes back into the petrol tank

st.reveal: Energy never vanishes. It changes form. Friction between the brake pads and the spinning discs turns the car's movement energy into heat. That's why brakes get hot, and why cars going down long mountain roads need to give their brakes a rest.

sec.t:
Most cars have disc brakes at least on the front wheels. A disc is a flat steel plate, a bit like a thick dinner plate, that turns with the wheel. A clamp called a caliper sits over its edge. When you brake, pistons in the caliper squeeze two pads onto either side of the disc, like fingers pinching a spinning coin.

Drum brakes, often on the back wheels of smaller cars, work from the inside. Curved shoes push outwards against the inside of a metal drum. A bicycle's rim brakes are a simple version of the same idea, with rubber blocks squeezing the wheel rim.

The front brakes do most of the work. When a car slows, its weight tips forward onto the front wheels, so they can grip harder.

Trains are far heavier than cars and harder to stop. Early trains relied on brakemen who ran along the roofs turning a wheel on each carriage. In 1869, the American inventor George Westinghouse patented an air brake. A pipe ran the length of the train, and air pressure worked the brakes on every carriage at once. A few years later he improved it, so that if the train split in two and the pipe broke, the brakes came on by themselves.

Air brakes are still used around the world, including on [[@indian-railways|Indian Railways]]. A long goods train can still need more than a kilometre to stop.

Electric cars and many electric trains have a trick. When the driver slows down, the motor is switched to work as a generator. The wheels turn the motor, which makes electricity, and that resistance slows the vehicle. This is called regenerative braking.

In an [[@electric-cars|electric car]], the electricity goes back into the battery. On electric trains, such as Mumbai's suburban trains and the [[@vande-bharat|Vande Bharat]] expresses, it can be fed back into the overhead wires for other trains to use. Ordinary [[friction|friction]] brakes are still there for hard stops and for the last few metres, when the motor can't do the job alone.

A system called ABS, now in most cars and many motorbikes, rapidly pulses the brakes in an emergency, many times a second. That stops the wheels locking and skidding, so the driver can steer around danger.

text: Most solids aren't slippery. Wood, stone and metal grip your shoes. Ice is different, because its surface doesn't behave like the rest of it.

The water [[molecule|molecules]] deep inside a block of ice are locked in a tidy pattern. The ones on the very top have no neighbours above them, so they're held less tightly. They wobble and roll about in a thin, loose layer only a few molecules thick. On top of that, when a skate or a shoe slides over ice, [[@friction|friction]] creates a little heat, which can melt a film of water.
Together, these make a slick surface that a skate blade glides over. Exactly how much each one contributes is still being studied.

st.reveal: A skater's weight lowers ice's melting point by only a fraction of a degree. That can't explain skating at minus 10 °C or colder. Scientists now point to a thin, loose layer of water molecules on the surface, plus melting from the heat of rubbing.

sec.t:
For more than a century, many textbooks said something different. They explained that a skater's weight, pressing down through a thin blade, melts the ice under it. The water then acts like oil.

It's true that pressure lowers the melting point of ice. But the effect is tiny. Even a heavy skater on a narrow blade lowers it by only a fraction of a degree. People skate happily on ice at minus 10 °C or colder, and you can slip on ice wearing wide, flat shoes. Pressure melting can't explain either. [[friction|Friction]] heating helps explain why a moving skate glides better than one standing still, but it doesn't explain why ice feels slippery the moment you step on it.

People have been skating for a very long time. [[archaeologist|Archaeologists]] have found skates made from animal leg bones in northern Europe, some probably several thousand years old. People tied them to their feet and pushed themselves along with sticks. Metal blades, which bite into the ice and let skaters steer, spread much later, especially in the Netherlands, where frozen canals made winter roads.

Today figure skating, speed skating and ice hockey are all part of the Winter [[@olympics|Olympics]]. The best speed skaters reach over 50 km/h, faster than many city cars.

sec.h: Skating on the roof of India
sec.t:
In winter, ponds and lakes in [[@ladakh|Ladakh]] freeze solid, and ice hockey has become one of the region's favourite sports. Children play on natural ice with hand-me-down skates, and teams from Ladakh have produced many of the players in India's national ice hockey squads, including the women's team.

Ice that's too smooth and wet, though, can be a hazard. Roads and pavements in cold places become dangerous in winter, which is why people spread grit and [[@salt-ice-roads|salt on icy roads]]. The same slippery surface that delights a skater can send a walker flying.

sec.t:
इतिहासकार इस संगीत को दौरों में बाँटते हैं। लगभग 1600 से 1750 तक के बारोक दौर में योहान सेबास्टियन बाख ने बहुत-सी धुनों को एक साथ बुना। आंतोनियो विवाल्दी ने *द फ़ोर सीज़न्स* लिखा, जिसका संगीत चिड़ियों, आँधी-तूफ़ान और सर्दी में ठिठुरने की नकल करता है।

लगभग 1750 से 1820 तक के क्लासिकल दौर में हेडन और मोत्सार्ट ने सुरुचिपूर्ण और संतुलित संगीत लिखा। सिम्फ़नी, यानी ऑर्केस्ट्रा के लिए कई हिस्सों वाली लंबी रचना, लोकप्रिय हुई। 1800 के दशक के रोमांटिक दौर में बीथोवन, शोपाँ और चाइकोव्स्की जैसे संगीतकारों ने अपने संगीत में गहरी भावनाएँ उड़ेल दीं। 20वीं सदी में संगीतकारों ने बहुत-से पुराने नियम तोड़े और नई आवाज़ों के साथ प्रयोग किए।

पश्चिमी शास्त्रीय संगीत आवाज़ की ऊँची-ऊँची मीनारें खड़ी करता है। संगीतकार वायलिन, चेलो, बाँसुरी, तुरही और ढोल के लिए अलग-अलग हिस्से लिख सकता है, हर कोई कुछ अलग बजाता है, और सब आपस में फ़िट हो जाते हैं। संचालक सामने खड़ा होकर ताल सँभालता है और प्रस्तुति को आकार देता है।

1824 में पहली बार बजी बीथोवन की नौवीं सिम्फ़नी के आख़िर में एक गायक-मंडली "ओड टू जॉय" गाती है। इसकी धुन आज यूरोपीय संघ का गान है। इस संगीत में हर जगह [[@maths-music|गणित]] छिपा है, साथ बजकर मीठे लगने वाले सुरों के अनुपातों से लेकर [[rhythm|लय]] के पैटर्न तक।

भारतीय संगीतकारों का पश्चिमी शास्त्रीय संगीत से पुराना नाता रहा है। 1936 में मुंबई में जन्मे ज़ुबिन मेहता दुनिया के सबसे जाने-माने संचालकों में से एक बने। उन्होंने 1978 से 1991 तक न्यूयॉर्क फ़िलहार्मोनिक की और लगभग 50 साल तक इज़राइल फ़िलहार्मोनिक की अगुवाई की।

मुंबई के एनसीपीए में स्थित सिम्फ़नी ऑर्केस्ट्रा ऑफ़ इंडिया 2006 में शुरू हुआ। पुराने बॉलीवुड स्टूडियो से लेकर [[@ar-rahman|ए. आर. रहमान]] तक, फ़िल्मी संगीतकारों ने अपने गानों में वायलिनों की टोलियाँ और पश्चिमी हार्मनी इस्तेमाल की है। सितार वादक [[@ravi-shankar|रवि शंकर]] ने सितार और ऑर्केस्ट्रा के लिए कॉन्चेर्तो लिखे, और दो महान परंपराओं को एक मंच पर ले आए।

text: In the USA, power is split into layers. There's the [[federal|federal]] government in Washington, D.C., then the 50 state governments, and below them a huge number of local governments. These include counties, cities, towns and villages, plus school districts and special districts that run things like water supply, fire services or public libraries.

Local governments handle the things you see every day: rubbish collection, street repairs, parks, local police and fire services, building rules, and most public schools. Many are led by elected mayors and councils. In some small towns, the residents still vote on decisions directly, in a town meeting.

Many everyday matters, such as rubbish collection, local roads, parks, zoning and most public schools, are decided by counties, cities, towns and school boards. Local elections often affect daily life more directly than national ones.

sec.t:
Almost every state is divided into counties, which run courts, keep records like births and land deeds, and often manage roads and jails. There are about 3,100 counties and similar areas in all. Texas alone has 254.

[[@new-orleans|Louisiana]] calls its counties parishes, a name left over from its French and Spanish Catholic past. Alaska calls them boroughs. A county may be led by an elected board and a sheriff, who heads local law enforcement. Americans elect many local officials that other countries would appoint, including sheriffs and, in most states, some judges and prosecutors.

Then there are special districts, set up for a single job. Some run airports or buses, some manage water, and in Florida several exist just to control [[@mosquito-diseases|mosquitoes]]. Each can have its own board and even collect its own taxes.

Cities usually have a mayor and a city council. In some, like New York and Chicago, the mayor is powerful and runs city departments directly. In others, the elected council hires a professional city manager to run things day to day.

City governments can be huge. New York City has more people than most American states and a budget larger than many countries'. Others are tiny. A town of a few hundred people might have a part-time mayor who also runs a shop.

Most American public schools are run by local school districts, each with an elected school board. There are around 13,000 of them. They hire superintendents, set school calendars and choose some of what is taught.

Much of the money comes from property taxes paid by local homeowners. This means schools in richer areas often have more money than those in poorer ones, a long-running debate in American life. India's [[@panchayat|panchayats]] and city councils do some of the same jobs, though Indian states play a bigger part in running schools. Turnout in local elections is often low, even though their decisions shape daily life most directly, from potholes to [[@police|policing]].

text: A minimum wage is the lowest pay an employer is allowed to give a worker by law. It is usually set per hour, per day or per month. If a factory, shop or farm pays less, it is breaking the law.

The idea is to stop workers from being paid so little that they cannot live decently, especially those with little bargaining power. Workers in strong [[@unions|trade unions]] can push for better pay together. A cleaner or a farm labourer working alone usually cannot, and the law steps in for them. In the USA, there is a national minimum and often higher state ones. In India, the central and state governments set minimum wages, which differ by state, by skill and by type of work.

st.reveal: David Card and Alan Krueger found no sign that the higher wage cut jobs. Other economists questioned their data and found different results in other studies. Card later shared a Nobel Prize for this kind of research.

Economists disagree. Some studies find small job losses, especially for young workers, while others find little effect. Much depends on how big the rise is compared with typical local wages.

sec.t:
India passed its Minimum Wages Act in 1948, just after independence. Instead of one number for the whole country, states set rates for many different jobs, from farm work to construction. There were once more than a thousand separate rates.

In 2019, Parliament passed the Code on Wages, which combines several old laws. It also allows a national "floor wage", a lowest level below which no state's minimum should fall. Still, many Indian workers are in informal jobs, such as street selling or domestic work, where wage laws are hard to enforce.

Most people agree that very low pay is a problem. The argument is about what a higher minimum wage does.

Some economists say that if labour costs more, businesses will hire fewer people, use more machines or raise prices. Young and less experienced workers might lose out. Others say higher pay means workers spend more, quit less often and work harder, so businesses can afford it.

In 1994, David Card and Alan Krueger compared fast-food restaurants in New Jersey, which had just raised its minimum wage, with those across the border in Pennsylvania. They found no drop in jobs. Other economists challenged their data, and the debate continues. Card shared the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2021, partly for this kind of natural experiment.

A minimum wage that never changes slowly loses value, because prices rise over time through [[@inflation|inflation]]. The US [[federal|federal]] minimum has been $7.25 an hour since 2009, so it buys much less than it did then. Many states, such as California and Washington, now set minimums more than twice as high.

Some places adjust their minimum wage automatically every year to match prices. Others leave it to politicians, which can mean long gaps between rises. Deciding the right number is partly maths and partly a judgment about fairness.

text: Carrom is a tabletop game where you flick a heavy disc, the striker, to knock smaller wooden pieces into the four corner pockets of a square board. One player sinks the white pieces, the other the black, and both chase a single red piece called the queen.

It became an Indian favourite because it needs very little: one board, a set of coins, a bit of powder and two or four people. It fits on a floor or a verandah, works in a power cut and keeps whole families busy on a rainy [[monsoon|monsoon]] afternoon. Many Indian homes, offices and housing societies have a board, often with the paint worn pale in the corners.

sec.t:
Nobody knows for sure. Most stories say carrom came from India, perhaps played in royal courts, and spread through South Asia. Some people link its name to a Portuguese word, carambola, also used for a type of shot in billiards. Firm records are hard to find, so the true start remains a mystery.

Similar flicking games appeared elsewhere too. Canada has crokinole and Latvia has novuss, played on bigger boards with cues. What is clear is that carrom became hugely popular in India, Sri Lanka and their neighbours in the 1900s. It then travelled with South Asian families to Britain, the Gulf and North America.

A standard board has a playing area about 74 cm on each side, roughly the width of a school desk, with a thick wooden frame around it. Players dust it with fine powder. The powder fills tiny bumps in the wood and lowers [[@friction|friction]], the force that slows sliding things down.

Too little powder and the coins drag. Too much and they skid off in every direction. Serious players fuss over it the way cricketers fuss over a pitch.

A good board is made of smooth plywood on a solid wooden frame, and it must stay perfectly flat. Players judge a board by how evenly the coins glide and how cleanly the striker bounces off the edge. Many families wipe it with a dry cloth and store it standing up, so it doesn't warp in the damp monsoon air.

{{story:friction}}

You sit at one side and place the striker on your baseline. You can only flick it with a finger, usually the index or middle finger, or the thumb. In doubles, four players sit around the board, with partners facing each other across it. The trick is in angles. A coin near the edge can be bounced, or banked, off the frame into a pocket, the same idea snooker players use.

The queen is worth extra points, but only if you cover it by pocketing one of your own pieces straight after. Sinking the striker by accident is a foul, and you have to give back one of your pieces. Like [[@chess-india|chess]], it rewards thinking a few moves ahead. Good players also leave the coins in awkward spots for their opponent, the way a snooker player leaves the cue ball tucked behind another ball.

In 1988 players from several countries formed the International Carrom Federation in Chennai, with agreed rules and board sizes. World championships and international [[tournament|tournaments]] followed, with India and Sri Lanka usually near the top.

Indian players such as Rashmi Kumari have won world titles. At the same time, carrom stays a home game, played next to [[@ludo|ludo]] and cards in summer holidays. In 2020, when the COVID-19 lockdowns kept families indoors, plenty of boards came down from the tops of cupboards and were dusted off again, powder and all.

यह कोशिका बँटकर दो बनती है, फिर चार, फिर आठ, और यह सिलसिला चलता रहता है। पहले आठ हफ़्तों को भ्रूण वाला दौर कहते हैं। इस दौरान ये कोशिकाएँ खुद को सजाकर दिल, दिमाग, रीढ़, हाथ और पैर बना लेती हैं। इसके बाद बच्चे को गर्भस्थ शिशु कहा जाता है, और बाकी के ज़्यादातर महीने बड़ा होने और हर [[organ|अंग]] को बाहर की ज़िंदगी के लिए तैयार करने में लगते हैं। आम गर्भावस्था लगभग 40 हफ़्ते चलती है। डॉक्टर इसे उस दिन से कुछ हफ़्ते पहले से गिनते हैं जब बच्चे की असल शुरुआत होती है।

sec.t:
पहले कुछ दिनों में कोशिकाओं की यह नन्ही गेंद गर्भाशय में पहुँचती है और उसकी मुलायम परत में जाकर बैठ जाती है। इनमें से कुछ कोशिकाएँ [[placenta|आँवल]] बनाने लगती हैं। आँवल, जिसे प्लेसेंटा भी कहते हैं, [[tissue|ऊतक]] की एक गद्दी है जो बच्चे को माँ के खून से जोड़ती है।

गर्भावस्था के लगभग छठे हफ़्ते तक एक नन्हा दिल धड़कने लगता है, जबकि भ्रूण बस कुछ मिलीमीटर लंबा होता है। हाथ-पैर बनने वाली कलियाँ उभर आती हैं। लगभग 10 हफ़्ते तक भ्रूण की उँगलियाँ बन जाती हैं, हाथों की भी और पैरों की भी, और तब से उसे गर्भस्थ शिशु कहा जाता है।

12 हफ़्ते पर गर्भस्थ शिशु लगभग एक नींबू जितना लंबा होता है, और सारे बड़े अंग बन चुके होते हैं। अगले महीनों में वह तेज़ी से बढ़ता है और उन कामों का अभ्यास करने लगता है जो उसे आगे चलकर करने हैं।

वह हिलता है, लात मारता है, अंगड़ाई लेता है। जिस पानी में वह तैरता है, उसे निगलता है, और उसे हिचकियाँ तक आती हैं। वह साँस लेने जैसी हरकतें करता है, हालाँकि उसके फेफड़ों में हवा नहीं, पानी भरा होता है। उसकी उँगलियों के सिरों पर बारीक लकीरें उभरती हैं, जो [[@fingerprints|उँगलियों की छाप]] बनाती हैं और ज़िंदगी भर वैसी ही रहती हैं। जिन [[@twins|जुड़वाँ]] के सारे जीन एक जैसे होते हैं, उनकी भी उँगलियों की छाप अलग-अलग होती है।

डॉक्टर [[ultrasound|अल्ट्रासाउंड]] से बढ़ते बच्चे की जाँच कर सकते हैं। एक यंत्र शरीर के भीतर बहुत ऊँची, बारीक आवाज़ भेजता है, इतनी ऊँची कि इंसान उसे सुन ही नहीं सकते। यह आवाज़ बच्चे से टकराकर लौटती है, कुछ-कुछ [[@echoes|गूँज]] की तरह, और कंप्यूटर इन गूँजों को एक तस्वीर में बदल देता है।

स्कॉटलैंड के डॉक्टर इयन डोनाल्ड ने 1950 के दशक में ग्लासगो में गर्भावस्था में अल्ट्रासाउंड के इस्तेमाल की शुरुआत की। आज भारत, अमेरिका और पूरी दुनिया में अल्ट्रासाउंड जाँच गर्भावस्था की देखभाल का आम हिस्सा है। चमगादड़ और डॉल्फ़िन भी यही तरकीब अपनाती हैं। वे आवाज़ भेजती हैं और गूँज सुनकर रास्ता ढूँढती हैं।

आखिरी हफ़्तों में बच्चे के शरीर पर चर्बी चढ़ती है, जो जन्म के बाद उसे गर्म रखती है, और उसके फेफड़े पूरी तरह तैयार हो जाते हैं। ज़्यादातर बच्चे घूमकर सिर नीचे कर लेते हैं। जन्म के समय बहुत-से बच्चे लगभग 50 सेमी लंबे और करीब 3 किलो के होते हैं, हालाँकि सेहतमंद बच्चों में भी काफ़ी फ़र्क होता है।

पहली बार रोते ही फेफड़ों में पहली बार हवा भरती है। दिल और खून की नलियाँ झटपट अपनी पाइपलाइन बदल लेती हैं, ताकि खून नाल की जगह फेफड़ों से होकर जाए। उसी पल से बच्चा खुद साँस लेने लगता है, और उसका [[@brain-development|दिमाग]] अपनी सबसे तेज़ बढ़त के सालों में कदम रखता है।

text: A digital footprint is the trail of information you leave behind when you use the internet. Every post, comment, photo, search and like adds to it. So does information collected quietly, such as which websites you visit, where your phone has been and what you buy.

Like footprints in wet cement, some of these marks can last for years. That isn't all bad. A footprint can also show off your projects, your art or your kindness. The trick is knowing it's there and choosing what goes into it.

st.prompt: You post a photo and delete it ten minutes later. Is it gone forever?

options.t: Not for sure, because others may have saved or copied it
Yes, deleting removes every copy at once
Yes, but only if the photo was private

st.reveal: Someone may have taken a screenshot or downloaded it in those ten minutes. Some apps and websites also keep backup copies for a while. That's why it helps to think before posting.

d.try: With a parent, search your own name, or a parent's name, in a search engine and look at the first page of results. Talk about which results the person posted themselves and which were posted by others. Then check the location setting on a family phone's camera.
myth: If you delete a post, it disappears forever.
Deleting removes it from your account, but screenshots, downloads, shares and backups can keep copies alive. Treat anything you post as something that might last.

sec.t:
Your active footprint is what you share on purpose. That includes a photo of your birthday cake, a review of a game or a message in a group chat. You can see these and, usually, delete them from your own account.

Your passive footprint is gathered without you noticing much. Websites record your visits. Apps log your location. Shops note what you browse. [[@search-engines|Search engines]] remember what you've looked for, to help them choose results and adverts. You can't see most of this, but companies can, and they often keep it for years.

Some information hides inside files. Photos from a phone can carry metadata, invisible notes that record the date, time and sometimes the exact location where they were taken. If location tagging is on, a photo of your front gate could reveal where you live.

Other clues are in plain sight but easy to miss. A school badge on a uniform, a street sign in the background or a bus number can tell strangers more than you meant to share. Even your device leaves a trace. Many websites can recognise a returning visitor from small details about their device and browser, without asking for a name.

Your footprint can affect how people see you. Some colleges and employers look up applicants online. A thoughtful project or a helpful post can impress them. A cruel joke from years ago might not.

Mean posts also hurt the people they're about. [[@cyberbullying|Cyberbullying]] can follow someone home on their phone, and nasty comments can be screenshotted and spread. Thinking before you post protects other people as well as yourself.

Laws are starting to give people more say. In 2014 a European court ruled that people can ask search engines to remove some old, irrelevant links about them, often called the right to be forgotten. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023 also lets people ask companies to erase their personal data in many cases.

You can help yourself too. Use private settings, turn off location for apps and cameras that don't need it, and ask before posting photos of friends. Talk to a trusted adult if something about you appears online that you don't like. Guarding your footprint is a big part of [[@privacy|privacy]], and a small habit now can save a lot of worry later. Many apps on [[@social-media|social media]] now let you see and download what they've stored about you, which is an eye-opening thing to try with a parent.

text: The first computers were enormous, noisy and slow by today's standards. Before them, "computers" were people, [[@usa-nasa-hidden-figures|often women]], who did long calculations by hand for [[astronomer|astronomers]], engineers and armies.

The first electronic computers were built in the 1940s. They filled whole rooms, used thousands of glass [[vacuum|vacuum]] tubes that glowed and often burned out, and were programmed by plugging in cables and flipping switches. They could do in seconds what took [[@moon-race-women|human computers]] days.
Within 30 years, [[transistor|transistors]] and microchips shrank computers from the size of a room to the size of a desk, and later to something that fits in your pocket.

st.prompt: How did people program ENIAC to do a new job in the 1940s?

options.t: By plugging cables and setting switches by hand, which could take days
By typing instructions on a keyboard
By speaking to it

st.reveal: ENIAC had no keyboard or screen. To set up a new problem, its programmers rewired it with cables and turned hundreds of switches. A team of six women worked out how to do this, often from wiring diagrams alone.

n.certNote: Historians argue about which machine was the "first computer", because it depends on what you count. Babbage's designs, Colossus, ENIAC and others each have a claim.

d.try: Become a human computer team. Give three friends a long list of additions, and split the work so one adds, one checks and one writes the answers neatly. Time how long it takes. Then do the same sums on a calculator and compare. This is how many calculations were done before electronic computers.
myth: Computer bugs got their name from a moth found inside an early computer.

Engineers were already calling faults "bugs" in Thomas Edison's time, in the 1870s. In 1947, a team working on the Harvard Mark II computer found a real moth in it and taped it in their logbook as a joke, because the word already existed.

sec.t:
People have built calculating machines for a very long time. Around 2,100 years ago, the ancient Greeks made the [[@antikythera|Antikythera mechanism]], a box of bronze gears that predicted [[@eclipses|eclipses]] and the positions of the Sun and Moon. It was found in a shipwreck in 1901.

In the 1800s, the English mathematician [[@charles-babbage|Charles Babbage]] designed steam-age machines of brass gears that could calculate and even follow programs on punched cards. He never finished building them, but his ideas came very close to a modern computer.

[[@world-war-two|The Second World War]] pushed computing ahead fast. In Britain, codebreakers at Bletchley Park built Colossus, finished in 1944. It helped read secret German messages. Its existence was kept secret for decades. The mathematician [[@alan-turing|Alan Turing]] also worked at Bletchley Park, on a different codebreaking machine.

In the USA, the Harvard Mark I, finished in 1944, was a giant calculator about 15 metres long, longer than a city bus. [[@grace-hopper|Grace Hopper]] was one of its first programmers.

sec.h: The tiny switch that changed everything
sec.t:
Vacuum tubes were big, hot and fragile. In 1947, scientists at Bell Labs in New Jersey invented the transistor, a small switch made from solid material with no glass and no glowing filament. By the 1960s, many transistors could be built together onto one chip.

Computers shrank, got cheaper and became more reliable. They guided [[@rockets-how|rockets]] and helped NASA reach the Moon. By the late 1970s, people could buy personal computers for their homes.

The first microprocessor, a whole processor on a single chip, went on sale in 1971. It was about the size of a fingernail yet did a similar amount of work to ENIAC, which had filled a room. Every computer since, from laptops to the chip in a toy, builds on that idea.

In 1956, the Indian Statistical Institute in [[@kolkata|Kolkata]] installed one of the first computers in India, to help with the huge calculations needed for planning and surveys.

In [[@mumbai|Mumbai]], scientists at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research decided to build one themselves. Their computer, called [[@tech-first-computer-india|TIFRAC]], was completed in 1960 using thousands of vacuum tubes. It was India's first home-built computer, and it helped train a generation of Indian engineers. Today India's computing industry employs millions, and its roots go back to rooms full of humming tubes.

text: A game engine is a big piece of software that does the basic jobs every video game needs. It draws the 3D world on screen, makes objects fall and bounce, plays sounds, and reacts when you press buttons. Game makers add their own art, characters, music and rules on top.

It's a bit like a kitchen. The engine provides the stove, the oven and the utensils. Each team cooks a different meal with them. Popular engines include Unreal, Unity and the free Godot, and many studios also build their own.

st.prompt: In many games, when a ball rolls off a table, how does the game decide where it goes?

options.t: The engine uses simplified physics maths to work out its path, frame by frame
An artist draws every possible fall by hand
The game copies a video of a real ball

st.reveal: The physics part of the engine applies rules like gravity and bouncing many times a second. It doesn't copy real physics perfectly, just closely enough to look right, which keeps the game running fast.

d.try: Make a flip book. On the corner of 20 pages of a small notebook, draw a ball falling and bouncing, moving it a little on each page. Flick the pages quickly. A game engine does the same thing, but draws each picture fresh, 60 or more times a second.
myth: Game makers write every part of every game from scratch.

Most games are built on an existing engine, either bought, free or made in-house and reused. That lets small teams focus on the story, art and rules instead of rebuilding basics like lighting and collisions.

30 to 60 or more frames per second

sec.t:
At the heart of every engine is a loop that repeats again and again, very fast. First it checks what the player is doing: which keys are pressed, where the controller is pointing. Then it updates the world: moves characters, applies [[@gravity-fall|gravity]], checks if anything has crashed into anything else. Finally it draws a new picture of the world on screen.

Each new picture is called a frame. A smooth game draws 60 or more frames a second. That leaves about 16 thousandths of a second for the whole loop. If the engine falls behind, the game stutters.

Real physics is complicated. A game can't calculate every grain of sand. So engines use shortcuts. A character might be treated as a simple capsule shape when checking for collisions. Water might be a moving texture rather than real drops.

The goal is to look and feel right while staying fast. Sometimes the shortcuts go wrong, which is why characters occasionally get stuck in walls or fly into the sky. Players love sharing these glitches.

In the early days, every game was built from scratch. In 1993 a company called id Software released *Doom*, and other studios paid to use its engine for their own games. That idea spread. Epic Games released Unreal Engine in 1998, and Unity followed in 2005, aiming to help small teams.

Today one engine might power thousands of games. Studios in Pune, Austin and everywhere in between use the same tools. A small Indian team in Pune made *Raji: An Ancient Epic*, a 2020 game set in a world drawn from Indian myths.

Engines are now used far outside gaming. For the [[@star-wars-effect|Star Wars]] series *The Mandalorian*, filmmakers surrounded actors with giant LED screens showing scenery drawn live by Unreal Engine. When the camera moved, the background shifted to match, which made [[@special-effects|special effects]] part of the filming itself.

Architects use engines to let clients walk through buildings before they're built. Car makers test driving software in virtual cities. And many young people first learn [[@programming|programming]] by making small games in free tools such as Scratch, which works like a simple engine for beginners.

text: A mobile network divides land into many small areas called cells, each served by a tower with antennas, called a base station. Your phone talks by [[@radio-waves|radio]] to the nearest tower.

From the tower, your call travels through cables to the network's central computers. These look up where the person you're calling is, then send your call to the tower nearest them. That tower passes it by radio to their phone. All of this happens in about a second, which is why the phone rings almost as soon as you dial.
If you move while talking, your call is handed from one tower to the next without dropping.

st.prompt: You call a friend in the USA from India. How does most of the call travel between the two countries?

options.t: Through fibre-optic cables laid on the sea floor
Bounced off a satellite in space
Through the air as one giant radio wave

st.reveal: Only the first and last short hops go by radio, between phones and nearby towers. In between, calls and internet data mostly travel as pulses of light through fibre-optic cables, including huge cables on the ocean floor. Satellites carry only a small share.

Most calls go by radio only to the nearest tower. From there they travel through cables, mostly fibre-optic, across land and under the sea. Satellites are used mainly in remote places, at sea and in the air.

sec.t:
Your SIM card holds a code that identifies you to the network. Every so often, even when you're not using it, your phone quietly tells nearby towers it's there. The network keeps a record of which area each phone is in.

When someone calls you, the network checks that record and asks the towers in your area to call your phone. Your phone answers, and the call is connected. For a call to another network or another country, the call passes between networks through exchanges and cables.

Your [[@voice|voice]] is turned into a stream of numbers by your phone. The phone squeezes this data to make it smaller, then sends it in tiny bursts by radio. At the other end, the numbers are turned back into sound.

This happens fast enough that the delay is usually too short to notice. Today, calls, messages and internet data all travel the same way, as packets of digital information.

The first mobile networks, in the 1980s, carried voices as analogue radio signals. They were called 1G later on. Phones were large and expensive. The second generation, 2G, in the 1990s, was digital and brought text messages. [[@5g|3G and 4G]] brought fast internet, so phones could show maps and videos. 5G, spreading through the 2020s, is faster again and can connect many more devices at once.

Before all this, phones used wires, as you can read in [[@telephone-history|the history of the telephone]].

India's first mobile phone call was made on 31 July 1995. Jyoti Basu, then [[@governors-states|chief minister]] of West Bengal, called the telecom minister, Sukh Ram, in Delhi from Writers' Building in [[@kolkata|Kolkata]]. Calls were costly at first, and mobile phones were a luxury.

Prices fell sharply over the next two decades. Today India has more than a billion mobile connections, and mobile data is among the cheapest in the world. Towers stretch from Himalayan villages to islands in the Bay of Bengal. In places no tower reaches, such as ships at sea, people rely on [[@satellites-help|satellites]] instead.

text: Nuclear fusion is when two very light [[atom|atoms]] crash together so hard that their centres, called [[nucleus|nuclei]], join into one heavier atom. A little bit of mass goes missing in the process, and it turns into a huge amount of energy. This is what [[@einstein|Einstein's]] famous equation, E = mc², describes.

Fusion powers the [[@sun-what|Sun]] and [[@star-life-cycle|every other star]]. In the Sun's core, hydrogen atoms fuse into helium, giving off the light and heat that reach us eight minutes later. Scientists have spent about 70 years trying to make fusion work on Earth as [[@future-energy|a clean source of electricity]]. It is one of the hardest engineering problems ever tackled.

st.prompt: Today's nuclear power stations, like those at Tarapur in India, make energy by which process?

options.t: Splitting big atoms apart (fission)
Joining small atoms together (fusion)
Burning uranium like coal

st.reveal: Every nuclear power station working today uses fission, splitting heavy atoms such as uranium. Fusion, joining light atoms, powers the Sun, but no power station has yet produced electricity from it.

d.try: Show why fusion is hard with two magnets. Push the same poles of two magnets toward each other and feel them shove apart. Atomic nuclei repel each other in a similar way, because they all carry positive charge. Only enormous heat and pressure can force them close enough to join.
myth: Nuclear power stations today run on fusion.

All working nuclear power stations use fission, which splits heavy atoms. Fusion is still in the experimental stage. Scientists hope it could one day give power with far less long-lasting radioactive waste.

sec.t:
All atomic nuclei carry positive electric charge, and like charges push each other away. To make two nuclei fuse, you have to slam them together fast enough to overcome that push.

The Sun manages this with crushing [[@gravity-fall|gravity]] and a core temperature of about 15 million °C. On Earth we can't copy the Sun's weight, so we make up for it with heat. Fusion machines must reach over 100 million °C. At that temperature, atoms break apart into a glowing soup of charged particles called [[plasma|plasma]]. No container could touch it without melting, and the plasma would cool and stop fusing the moment it touched a wall. The fuel is usually two heavier kinds of hydrogen, called deuterium and tritium, which fuse more easily than ordinary hydrogen.

sec.h: Holding a star in a magnetic bottle

sec.t:
There is another approach. At the National Ignition Facility in California, 192 giant [[@lasers|lasers]] fire at a fuel pellet smaller than a peppercorn, crushing and heating it in a billionth of a second.

In an experiment on 5 December 2022, for the first time, the fusion reaction there released more energy than the lasers delivered to the fuel. It was a historic moment. But the lasers themselves needed far more electricity from the grid than the reaction produced, so there is still a long road to a working power station.

Fusion fuel can come from seawater and from lithium, so supplies would last a very long time. Fusion makes no [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]] while running, so it would not add to [[@climate-change|climate change]]. It also can't run out of control the way some people fear, because if anything goes wrong, the plasma simply cools and stops.

Scientists like to joke that fusion power has been "30 years away" for decades. Many private companies now say they will do it sooner. Others are more cautious. If it works, fusion could one day give the world electricity from the same process that lights the stars.

text: A smart home is a home where everyday devices are connected to a network, usually Wi-Fi, so they can be controlled from a phone, by voice or automatically. Lights can switch on when you walk in. An air conditioner can cool a room before you get home. A doorbell camera can show who's at the gate while you're at school.

Each smart device has [[sensor|sensors]], a tiny computer and a radio to talk to the network. Many also connect to the company's computers far away, called [[server|servers]], which do the heavy thinking. Smart homes can save effort and energy and help people who find switches hard to reach. They also raise real questions about privacy and safety.

st.prompt: A smart speaker is waiting for its wake word, like "Alexa". What is it doing with the sound in the room?

options.t: Listening on the device itself and throwing the sound away until it hears the wake word
Sending every word to the company's computers all the time
Recording everything onto a memory card

st.reveal: The speaker runs a small program that only listens for its wake word. When it thinks it hears it, it starts sending audio to the company's servers. It sometimes wakes by mistake on similar-sounding words, which is one reason people worry about privacy.

Mark which ones connect to the internet or an app. Then, with an adult, check whether the router and any cameras still use the password they came with. Changing default passwords is one of the simplest ways to keep a home safer.
myth: Smart speakers record everything you say, all day long.

They listen locally for their wake word and only start sending audio when they think they hear it. But they do sometimes wake by accident, and companies have used recorded clips to improve their systems, so privacy settings are worth checking.
facts: it connects to a network and can be controlled remotely or automatically
speakers, bulbs, plugs, cameras, locks, thermostats, robot vacuums
Matter, a shared standard so brands work together

sec.t:
People have imagined automatic homes for a long time. World fairs in the 1930s and 1950s showed "homes of tomorrow" with push-button kitchens. In the 1970s, a system called X10 let people switch lamps on and off by sending signals through a house's electrical wiring.

The modern smart home took off in the 2010s. Cheap chips, fast [[@wifi|Wi-Fi]] and smartphones arrived together. In 2011, a thermostat that learned a family's habits went on sale in the USA. In 2014, Amazon launched the Echo speaker with its voice assistant, Alexa. Soon there were smart bulbs, plugs, locks, cameras, fridges and robot [[vacuum|vacuum]] cleaners. All of them belong to a bigger trend called the [[@internet-of-things|Internet of Things]].

Most smart devices follow a simple pattern: sense, decide, act. A motion sensor notices someone in the hallway. A rule, set up in an app, says "if motion after sunset, turn on the light". The bulb switches on.

[[@voice-assistants|Voice assistants]] add speech. When you say "Alexa, turn off the fan", the speaker records the request and sends it to a server. Software there turns the sound into words, works out what you mean and sends a command back to the fan's smart plug. It all happens in a second or two.

{{story:voice-assistants}}

For years, devices from different companies often refused to work together. In 2022, many big tech firms launched Matter, a shared standard meant to let a bulb from one brand obey a speaker from another.

For someone who uses a wheelchair, or an older person with shaky hands, being able to say "lock the door" or "switch on the lights" can make daily life much easier. Smart [[@smoke-alarms|smoke alarms]] can send a warning to a phone, even if nobody is at home.

In India, smart plugs are popular for turning on water heaters before a bath and for scheduling air conditioners. Voice assistants now understand Hindi and several other Indian languages, so you don't need to speak English to use them.

A home full of microphones and cameras collects a lot of information. Companies may store recordings and data about when you come and go. That makes [[@privacy|privacy]] a big issue, and it's worth checking what each device records.

Security is the other worry. In 2016, a malicious program called Mirai searched the internet for cameras and routers still using factory passwords like "admin". It took over hundreds of thousands of them and used them together to flood websites with traffic, knocking popular services offline for hours.

There's also the question of what happens when a company gives up. In 2022, a US smart-home firm called Insteon shut its servers down with almost no warning, and many customers' lights and switches stopped working through the app overnight. A smart home, it turns out, is only as reliable as the company and the network behind it.

text: Wilbur and Orville Wright learned to fly by studying, testing and practising, step by step, for about four years. They were bicycle makers from Dayton, Ohio, with no university training in engineering. They read everything about flight they could find, watched birds, built kites and [[@gliders|gliders]], and even made their own wind tunnel.

Their big insight was that the hard part of flying was not lifting off but controlling the machine in the air. On 17 December 1903, near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville made the first powered, controlled flight. It lasted 12 seconds. By the end of that day, Wilbur had flown for 59 seconds.

st.prompt: The Wrights worked out how to steer by watching birds. What did they notice?

options.t: Birds twist the tips of their wings to tilt and turn
Birds steer mostly by moving their heads
Birds flap faster on one side to turn

st.reveal: The brothers saw that birds tilt by twisting their wing tips, raising one side and lowering the other. They copied this with "wing warping", using wires to twist the Flyer's wings. Modern planes do the same job with hinged flaps called ailerons.

n.certNote: Most historians credit the Wright brothers with the first controlled, sustained, powered aeroplane flight in 1903. Supporters of other early aviators, such as Alberto Santos-Dumont in Brazil and Gustave Whitehead in the USA, argue for their claims, but the Wrights' evidence is by far the strongest.

The second plane should roll and turn, because the wings now push the air differently, the same idea the Wrights used to steer.

People had flown in hot-air balloons since 1783, and gliders had carried people before the Wrights. The Wrights made the first controlled, sustained flight in a powered aeroplane that was heavier than air.

about 12 horsepower, built by their mechanic Charlie Taylor

sec.t:
The Wrights' interest in flight started young. In 1878 their father brought home a small toy helicopter powered by a twisted rubber band. The boys played with it until it broke, then built copies.

As adults they ran the Wright Cycle Company, building and repairing [[@bicycles-history|bicycles]]. The work taught them about light, strong frames, chains and balance. A bicycle is unstable until a rider controls it. They guessed an aeroplane would be the same: a pilot would need to keep balancing it all the time.

No company could sell them a light enough engine, so their mechanic, Charlie Taylor, built one from [[@aluminium|aluminium]] in about six weeks. The brothers carved their own [[propeller|propellers]], treating them as spinning wings.

On the cold, windy morning of 17 December 1903, they took turns. Orville went first, lying on the lower wing. The Flyer lifted, swooped and landed about 37 m away after 12 seconds, less than the length of many modern jets. Only five local people were there to watch. On the fourth flight, Wilbur flew about 260 m in 59 seconds before a gust of wind damaged the plane.

At first few people believed them. [[@newspapers|Newspapers]] ignored or doubted the story. The brothers kept improving their planes in a field near Dayton. In 1908, Wilbur flew in public in France, making smooth turns and figure-of-eight loops. Crowds were astonished, and the Wrights became world-famous.

Flight spread fast. In February 1911, a French pilot [[@hist-first-flight-india|flew bags of mail]] about 10 km from Allahabad across the Yamuna to Naini, the first official airmail flight anywhere. In 1932, J.R.D. Tata flew mail from Karachi to Bombay, the start of what became Air India.

The original 1903 Flyer now hangs in the [[@smithsonian|Smithsonian]] National Air and Space Museum in Washington, D.C. Pieces of its fabric have travelled with [[@apollo-moon|Apollo 11]] to the Moon and with NASA's [[@mars-helicopter|Ingenuity helicopter]] to [[@mars-rovers|Mars]], where in 2021 it made the first powered flight on another planet.

text: Leave an iron nail outside through one Indian [[monsoon|monsoon]] and it turns orange and flaky. Yet the iron pillar in Delhi's Qutb complex has stood in the open for about 1,600 years and still looks almost smooth. It is about as tall as a two-storey house and weighs more than 6 tonnes, about as much as an adult elephant.

The secret is in the iron itself. The smiths who made it left a lot of phosphorus in the metal. Over time, that phosphorus helped a very thin, very tight layer form on the surface. This layer works like a raincoat, keeping water and air away from the iron underneath.

st.prompt: What keeps the Delhi iron pillar from rusting away?

options.t: A thin protective layer that formed on its surface, helped by phosphorus in the iron
A secret paint the Gupta smiths brushed on
Delhi's air is too dry for anything to rust

st.reveal: Phosphorus in the iron helped a thin, tight layer of iron compounds grow on the surface. That layer seals the metal underneath. Delhi's dry months help, but the pillar has faced about 1,600 monsoons.

src: Balasubramaniam R. (2002) Delhi Iron Pillar. Indian Institute of Advanced Study / IIT Kanpur.

myth: The iron pillar never rusts at all.

It does rust, just very slowly and only on the surface. A thin protective layer stops the rust from eating deeper. The part of the pillar once buried in damp soil has corroded more than the part in the air.

sec.t:
An [[inscription|inscription]] in Sanskrit, cut into the pillar in an old script, praises a king called Chandra. Most historians think this was Chandragupta II, one of the great rulers of the [[@gupta-golden-age|Gupta age]], around 400 CE. The pillar once had a statue of Garuda on top, the bird who carries the god Vishnu.

Here is the twist: the pillar probably didn't start in Delhi. Many scholars think it first stood somewhere in central India, possibly near Udayagiri in Madhya Pradesh, and was moved to Delhi centuries later. Nobody knows exactly how a 6-tonne pillar was carried hundreds of kilometres.

sec.h: How do you make 6 tonnes of iron without a factory?
The thin layer that saved it
sec.t:
[[@rust|Rust]] is iron joining with oxygen and water. Normal rust is loose and crumbly. It flakes off, exposing fresh iron, which rusts again, and so on until the metal is gone.

In 2002, the metallurgist R. Balasubramaniam at IIT Kanpur studied the pillar closely. He found a protective film only about one-twentieth of a millimetre thick. It contains iron, oxygen, hydrogen and phosphorus, packed tightly together. One compound in it, called misawite, fills the gaps so water can't sneak through. Delhi's long dry months, when the pillar can dry out completely, help too.

For generations, visitors had a tradition: stand with your back to the pillar and try to wrap your arms around it. If your fingers met, people said, you would have good luck. So many hands rubbed the pillar that the lower part became shiny and worn.

In 1997, a fence was put around it to protect it. Today you can only look. Nearby is a dent where some say a cannonball struck in the 1700s, and the pillar shrugged it off. And there's another iron pillar story: a much larger broken one lies at Dhar in Madhya Pradesh, and it too has resisted rust. Yet both are youngsters: smiths in India were already smelting iron about 3,000 years ago, in what we now call the [[@iron-age|Iron Age]].

text: The Golden Temple is the holiest gurdwara, or Sikh place of worship, in the world. Its proper name is Harmandir Sahib, "the temple of God". It stands in the middle of a large pool in the city of [[@amritsar|Amritsar]], in Punjab, and its upper floors are covered in gold.

Inside, the Sikh holy book, the [[@guru-granth-sahib|Guru Granth Sahib]], is read aloud and sung from early morning until night. The temple is open to people of every religion. Millions visit each year. Many also come to eat at its langar, a free kitchen where anyone can sit down for a meal.

st.prompt: Why does the Golden Temple have four entrances, one on each side?

options.t: To show that people from every direction and background are welcome
Because four rivers flow into its pool
To let four kings enter at once

st.reveal: Sikh teaching says that God belongs to everyone equally. The four doors are a sign that people of any religion, caste or country can enter.

n.certNote: The main dates of the temple are well recorded. A popular tradition says the Sufi saint Mian Mir laid its foundation stone, but historians debate this because early sources don't mention it.

d.try: Hold a mini langar at home. Everyone sits on the floor in a row, whatever their age, and is served the same simple meal by someone else. Afterwards, everyone helps clean up. Talk about how it felt to eat side by side instead of at the head of a table.
myth: You have to be a Sikh to enter the Golden Temple.
The temple is open to everyone, of any faith or none. Visitors only need to cover their heads, remove their shoes, wash their feet and follow simple rules like not smoking or drinking alcohol.
