sec.t:
The fourth Sikh Guru, Guru Ram Das, began digging a pool here in the 1570s. It was called Amrit Sarovar, "the pool of [[nectar|nectar]]", and the town around it became Amritsar.

His son, Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, built the temple in the middle of the pool. Tradition says the Sufi saint Mian Mir of Lahore was invited to lay the foundation stone in 1588, though historians debate whether that happened. In 1604 Guru Arjan placed the first version of the Sikh [[scripture|scripture]], the Adi Granth, inside.

The temple sits lower than the land around it, so visitors walk down steps to reach it. This is often explained as a lesson in humility.

The temple was attacked and badly damaged several times in the 1700s, including by the Afghan ruler Ahmad Shah Durrani in 1762. Sikhs rebuilt it each time.

In the early 1800s, [[@ranjit-singh|Maharaja Ranjit Singh]], who ruled Punjab, paid for the upper floors to be covered with gilded copper and decorated with marble and fine inlay work. That's when visitors began calling it the Golden Temple. The gold is still cleaned and restored by skilled craftspeople.

Next to the temple is the langar hall. Every day, people sit together on long mats on the floor and are served dal, roti, a vegetable dish and kheer. Everyone eats the same food, whether rich or poor, Sikh or not.

The kitchen serves tens of thousands of meals a day, and on festival days the numbers are often reported to pass a lakh. Most of the work is done by [[@volunteering|volunteers]], who chop vegetables, roll rotis, serve food and wash plates. Machines help make rotis now, but huge numbers are still rolled by hand. The idea of langar comes from Guru Nanak, the first Guru, who taught that sharing food breaks down barriers between people.

sec.h: A place of history and of pain
sec.t: The complex also includes the Akal Takht, the highest seat of Sikh authority. In 1984, during an Indian Army operation against armed militants who had taken position inside the complex, the Akal Takht was badly damaged and many people died. The event still causes deep pain for many Sikhs, and the Akal Takht was later rebuilt.

Every morning before dawn, the Guru Granth Sahib is carried from its resting place to the temple in a decorated palanquin. Late at night it is carried back. Between those times, the hymns never stop.

At night the temple's gold reflects in the still water of the pool, and the [[@punjabi-food|Punjabi]] cooks next door are already getting tomorrow's dal ready.

text: India has 28 states and 8 union [[territory|territories]], and each has its own mix of landscape, language, food and festivals. A simple way to make sense of them is to think in regions. There's the mountainous north, the green northeast, the river plains of the east, the dry west, the forested centre and the southern [[peninsula|peninsula]].

Within each region, states often have their own main language. That's not an accident. In 1956, most state borders were redrawn around language areas. So when you cross from [[@kerala|Kerala]] into Tamil Nadu, or from Gujarat into Maharashtra, the signboards usually change script.

st.prompt: In 1956, India redrew the borders of most of its states. What was the main idea behind the new borders?

options.t: Keeping people who spoke the same language together
Making every state roughly the same size
Following the old borders of British provinces exactly

st.reveal: The States Reorganisation Act of 1956 drew many borders around language areas. That is why, for example, Kannada is the main language of Karnataka and Telugu of Andhra Pradesh. Some states were split again later, such as Telangana in 2014.

myth: Everyone in India speaks Hindi.

Hindi is the most widely spoken language, but hundreds of millions of Indians speak another language at home, such as Bengali, Marathi, Telugu, Tamil, Gujarati or Kannada. India's Constitution lists 22 languages, and many more are spoken.

sec.t:
At the top of the map, the Himalaya rise above Jammu and Kashmir, [[@ladakh|Ladakh]], Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand. Winters are snowy, houses have sloping roofs, and apples and walnuts grow on the hillsides.

Below them lie the wide, flat plains of Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, watered by rivers that start in the [[glacier|glaciers]]. These plains grow much of India's wheat and rice, and many of India's oldest cities, such as Varanasi and Patna, grew up beside their rivers. Uttar Pradesh alone had about 20 crore people at the 2011 [[census|census]], more than most countries.

Rajasthan, India's largest state by area, is home to much of the [[@thar-formed|Thar Desert]] and a famous ring of hilltop forts. Gujarat has a long coastline and the [[@earth-salt-flats|salt flats]] of the [[@gujarat-rann|Rann of Kutch]]. Maharashtra holds Mumbai, the country's money capital, and the green hills of the Western Ghats.

In the middle, [[@madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]] and Chhattisgarh are thick with forests, tigers and ancient rock paintings. [[@india-wonder-goa-history|Goa, the smallest state]], sits on the western coast, with a long history of Portuguese rule that still shows in its churches and food.

In the east, West Bengal and [[@odisha|Odisha]] face the Bay of Bengal. Kolkata was once the capital of British India, and Odisha is known for the Konark Sun Temple and Rath Yatra.

The south is a large plateau, called the Deccan, edged by coasts. Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana each have their own Dravidian language with its own script, such as Kannada, Tamil, [[@malayalam|Malayalam]] and Telugu. Rice, coconut and lentil batters turn up in many [[@regional-cuisines|southern dishes]], and tall temple towers rise above the towns.

Even the year starts differently across India. Many people in Punjab celebrate Baisakhi, in Assam [[@art-bihu|Bohag Bihu]] and in Tamil Nadu Puthandu, all in mid-April. People in Gujarat often mark the new year the day after Diwali. Map out India's festivals and you get a map of its [[@states-india|states]]: each one familiar to its own people, and new to everyone else.

text: Chocolate gets its melt from cocoa butter, the natural fat in cacao beans. In a well-made bar, this fat is set into tiny crystals that melt at about 34°C. Your mouth is about 36 to 37°C, slightly warmer. So on your tongue the crystals collapse, and the solid square becomes a smooth, thick liquid in seconds.

Your fingers are usually a few degrees cooler, so chocolate holds its shape in your hand for a little while. In a hot car or a summer pocket it gives up completely. Chocolate makers work hard to get that melting point just right.

st.prompt: Why does a square of chocolate stay firm in your fingers for a while but melt fast on your tongue?

options.t: Cocoa butter melts just below mouth temperature, and your fingers are cooler than your mouth
Saliva contains a chemical that dissolves chocolate
Chewing makes friction that heats it up

st.reveal: The skin of your fingers is usually a few degrees cooler than the inside of your mouth. Well-made chocolate melts at about 34°C, so it holds its shape in the hand for a little while and turns liquid on the tongue.

myth: Chocolate with white or grey streaks has gone bad.
Those streaks are called bloom. Fat or sugar has risen to the surface after the chocolate got warm or damp. It looks dull and may feel crumbly, but it is safe to eat.

sec.t:
Cocoa butter is fussy. As it cools, its fat [[molecule|molecules]] can stack up in six different patterns, called crystal forms. Each form has a different melting point, from about 17°C to about 36°C.

Only one, known as form V, gives everything people want. It melts at about 34°C, has a glossy shine and snaps cleanly when broken. The other forms make chocolate that is dull, soft, crumbly or greasy. Chocolate left to cool any old way ends up with a messy mix.

Melting takes energy. As chocolate turns liquid on your tongue, it soaks up heat from your mouth, so it can feel slightly cool, like a tiny ice cube. The same thing happens when ice melts in a drink, or when [[@evaporation-cooling|sweat evaporates]] from your skin.

Chocolate also melts smoothly because its particles are ground very fine. In 1879, the Swiss maker Rodolphe Lindt invented conching, where liquid chocolate is churned for hours, sometimes days. Before that, chocolate bars were gritty. After it, they melted like silk.

sec.h: From hot drink to solid bar
sec.t:
For most of its history, chocolate was not eaten at all. The Olmec, [[@aztecs-maya|Maya]] and Aztecs of Mexico and Central America drank it, often frothy, bitter and spiced with chilli. Cacao beans were valuable enough to be used as money.

Europeans sweetened the drink with sugar. Then, in 1847, the English company J. S. Fry and Sons sold one of the first moulded chocolate bars. Milk chocolate followed in Switzerland in the 1870s. Today, cacao also grows in southern India, especially in Kerala, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh, often in the shade of coconut and areca palms.

Melting is a problem in hot countries. During the Second World War, the US Army asked Hershey's to make a ration bar that would not melt in a soldier's pocket. It was thick, hard and, by most accounts, not very tasty.

Modern companies have tried heat-resistant chocolates for [[tropical|tropical]] markets, usually by changing the recipe or the fats. But the melt is half the pleasure. Chocolate also contains a mild stimulant called theobromine, which is why it is poisonous to dogs. And the strangest part is where it starts: the pods grow straight out of the trunk of the [[@chocolate-tree|cacao tree]], as if someone had glued them on.

text: Thali simply means plate. But in Indian food, a thali is also a complete meal served on one large plate, usually made of steel, brass or a [[@south-indian-meals|banana leaf]]. Small bowls called katoris sit around the edge, filled with dal, vegetables, curd and more. Rice or rotis go in the middle, with [[@pickles-achar|pickle]], [[@papad|papad]] and a sweet on the side.

The idea is balance. A thali gives you a bit of everything: grains, [[@pulses-dal|pulses]], vegetables and dairy, and many different tastes in one sitting. Every region of India has its own version, so a thali in Gujarat looks very different from one in Bengal.

st.prompt: In Kerala, the grand Onam feast called sadya is traditionally served on what?

options.t: A banana leaf
A silver plate
A large wooden board

st.reveal: A sadya is served on a long banana leaf, with dishes placed in a set order. Guests eat with their right hand, and folding the leaf afterwards is a way of showing you enjoyed the meal.

Many Indian dishes are mild. Curd rice, plain dal, khichdi, many sweets and Gujarati dishes are gentle and often a little sweet. Chilli heat varies hugely from region to region and from family to family.

A typical north Indian thali might hold rotis, rice, dal, two vegetable dishes, [[@cheese-paneer|paneer]], raita, pickle, salad and a small sweet like [[@food-gulab-jamun|gulab jamun]]. Eating it is a little like a journey: you mix a bite of dal with rice, then a bite of sabzi with roti, then a spoon of curd.

Many restaurants serve "unlimited thalis", where servers keep refilling the bowls until you say stop. In Gujarati and Rajasthani restaurants, the server often comes round with buckets, ladling more dal before you have asked.

Ayurveda, India's traditional system of medicine, describes six tastes: sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter and astringent. Ayurvedic texts suggest that a good meal includes all six for balance.

Whether or not people follow Ayurveda, many thalis do cover all six. There is sweet kheer, sour pickle or kadhi, salty papad, pungent chutney, bitter methi or karela, and astringent foods like pomegranate or some leafy greens.

India's regions each fill the plate differently. A Gujarati thali has dal and kadhi that are gently sweet, along with [[@gujarati-food|dhokla]] and farsan snacks. A Rajasthani thali might feature dal baati churma and ker sangri, a dish of desert berries and beans.

In Bengal, a meal may come in courses, starting with bitter shukto and ending with mishti doi. Maharashtra has varan bhaat and puran poli. In Punjab, you might find [[@punjabi-food|sarson ka saag]] with makki ki roti.

In 2020, India's Economic Survey, a yearly report by the Ministry of Finance, included a chapter called "Thalinomics". It studied how much a simple vegetarian or non-vegetarian thali cost compared with what a worker earned. The survey found that a thali had become more affordable for workers over the previous decade or so.

Indian restaurants in the United States often serve thalis, especially at lunch. Many Americans meet the idea there for the first time. A home-cooked [[@rice|rice]] and dal meal, packed into a tiffin, is also what [[@mumbai|Mumbai]]'s [[@lunchbox-dabbawala|dabbawalas]] carry across the city every day. Wherever it is served, a thali is a small map of the kitchen it came from.
